title: Round-Robin Pure Nash Equilibria Are Envy-Free Up to One Good Towards Agents Receiving at Most Two Goods
abstract: Do pure Nash equilibria in the Round-Robin picking-sequence mechanism satisfy envy-freeness up to one good (EF1)? While a published claim asserting that all pure Nash equilibria are EF1 was refuted by a counterexample with $2n+2$ goods, the property survives in part: in every pure Nash equilibrium with nonnegative additive valuations, an agent is EF1 towards any agent who appears at most twice in the picking sequence. The proof analyzes the sequence structure to show that if an envied agent receives two goods, at least one remains unallocated before the envying agent's first turn; deviating to rank that good first secures it, which under the equilibrium condition bounds the envy. As a consequence, every pure Nash equilibrium with at most $2n$ goods is EF1. This result is verified in Lean as `round_robin_pne_ef1_pair_of_count_le_two`.
introduction:
In the fair division of indivisible goods among $n$ agents with additive valuations, the Round-Robin picking sequence is a standard mechanism where agents take turns selecting their most preferred available item in the cyclic order $(1, 2, \dots, n, 1, 2, \dots)$. When agents strategically report rankings over goods, their behavior is captured by the pure Nash equilibria of the picking-sequence game. A standard fairness benchmark in this setting is envy-freeness up to one good (EF1), requiring that any envy an agent feels towards another can be eliminated by removing at most one good from the other agent's bundle.

A published claim stated that every pure Nash equilibrium of the Round-Robin mechanism with nonnegative additive valuations is EF1. However, this claim was corrected by a paper that presented a counterexample with $n$ agents and $2n + 2$ goods where an equilibrium allocation fails to be EF1.

Despite this counterexample, the claim was known to hold in restricted cases: `round_robin_pne_ef1_of_card_le_two_mul` shows that with $n$ agents and at most $2n$ goods, every pure Nash equilibrium of Round-Robin is EF1, as every agent picks at most twice.

This post presents the Lean-verified theorem `round_robin_pne_ef1_pair_of_count_le_two`, which establishes that the EF1 property holds pairwise. For any number of agents and goods, in any pure Nash equilibrium with nonnegative additive valuations, any agent $i$ is EF1 towards any agent $j$ who appears at most twice in the picking sequence. Thus, the published claim survives in part: non-EF1 envy can only occur towards agents who receive at least three goods.
result:
Let $n$ and $m$ be positive natural numbers, representing the number of agents and goods. Valuations are additive with non-negative weights $w(i, g) \ge 0$, lifted to valuations via `SocialChoice.FairDivision.Indivisible.AdditiveValuation.toValuation`. A strategy profile $\text{rank}$ is a pure Nash equilibrium of the picking-sequence mechanism `round_robin_sequence`, defined by `is_picking_sequence_pne`, meaning no agent can strictly improve their true bundle valuation by unilaterally changing their reported ranking. Let $A_k = \text{picking\_sequence\_outcome}(\text{round\_robin\_sequence}(n, m), \text{rank}, k)$ be the bundle received by agent $k$.

The theorem `round_robin_pne_ef1_pair_of_count_le_two` proves that for any two distinct agents $i$ and $j$, if agent $j$ appears at most twice in the round-robin sequence and receives a non-empty bundle $A_j$, then agent $i$ is EF1 towards agent $j$: there exists an item $g \in A_j$ such that
$$v_i(A_j \setminus \{g\}) \le v_i(A_i).$$

The Lean statement formalizes this by quantifying over $n, m : \mathbb{N}$ with $[NeZero\ n]$, an additive weight matrix $w : \text{Fin } n \to \text{Fin } m \to \mathbb{R}$ with $hw : \forall i\ g, 0 \le w\ i\ g$, ranking profile $rank$, the equilibrium hypothesis $h$, distinct agents $i, j : \text{Fin } n$, the turn bound $hj : (\text{round\_robin\_sequence } n\ m).\text{count } j \le 2$, and non-emptiness $hne : A_j.\text{Nonempty}$, concluding the existential EF1 condition.

This result strengthens `round_robin_pne_ef1_of_card_le_two_mul`, which required the global condition $m \le 2n$ so that all agents pick at most twice, by showing that EF1 holds between any pair $(i, j)$ whenever agent $j$ individually picks at most twice, even if other agents pick more often.
proof:
The proof analyzes the size of agent $j$'s bundle $A_j$ relative to their turns in the sequence. If $|A_j| \le 1$, removing the single good leaves the empty set, which trivially satisfies EF1 since valuations are non-negative. If $|A_j| > 1$, then $|A_j| = 2$ and agent $j$ appears twice, while before agent $i$'s first turn, agent $j$ has received at most one item. This ensures that some item $b \in A_j$ is completely unallocated when agent $i$ first picks, so agent $i$ could deviate to rank $b$ first and secure it; by pure Nash equilibrium, agent $i$'s bundle must be worth at least as much as this deviation, and removing the other item $a \in A_j$ leaves $\{b\}$, establishing EF1.

The steps proceed as follows:

- The additive valuation is unfolded into sums over bundles, and shorthand is defined for the sequence, rankings, initial empty state, and bundles $A$. Because individual item weights are non-negative, the sum of weights over any bundle is non-negative for agent $i$.
- In the case $|A_j| \le 1$, since $A_j$ is non-empty, it contains some item $g$. Removing $g$ leaves $A_j \setminus \{g\} = \emptyset$. The empty set has value $0$, which is at most $v_i(A_i)$.
- When $|A_j| > 1$, since the number of items received cannot exceed turns in the sequence, $2 \le |A_j| \le \text{count}(j, \text{seq}) \le 2$, so $|A_j| = 2$ and $\text{count}(j, \text{seq}) = 2$. If $m \le n$, the sequence is a prefix of length at most $n$ where every agent appears at most once, forcing $\text{count}(j, \text{seq}) \le 1$, a contradiction. Thus $n < m$, so agent $i$'s first turn occurs at index $i < n < m$.
- Let $st_0$ be the state before agent $i$'s first turn (after prefix length $i$). In this prefix, agent $j$ appears at most once, so $j$ holds at most one item at $st_0$. Monotonicity of picking turns ensures that bundles at $st_0$ are subsets of final bundles.
- Because $|A_j| = 2$ while $j$ has at most one item at $st_0$, there is some $b \in A_j$ not held by $j$ at $st_0$. If $b$ were held by any other agent $a \ne j$ at $st_0$, monotonicity would put $b \in A_a$, contradicting bundle disjointness. Thus $b$ is unallocated before turn $i$.
- Consider the deviated ranking $r'$ for agent $i$ that swaps $b$ to the top position. Because agent $i$ has no turns before index $i$, updating $i$'s ranking leaves the process up to $st_0$ unchanged. At turn $i$, item $b$ is available and top-ranked, so agent $i$ picks $b$. By monotonicity, $b$ remains in agent $i$'s final bundle under this deviation.
- Because $|A_j| > 1$, there exists an item $a \in A_j$ distinct from $b$. Since $|A_j| \le 2$, $A_j$ contains no other elements, so $A_j \setminus \{a\} = \{b\}$, which has value $w(i, b)$.
- By the pure Nash equilibrium condition $h$, agent $i$'s equilibrium valuation $v_i(A_i)$ is at least their valuation under deviation $r'$. Since weights are non-negative, the single item $b$ is worth at most the deviated bundle. Transitivity gives $v_i(A_j \setminus \{a\}) = w(i, b) \le v_i(A_i)$.
discussion:
The theorem `round_robin_pne_ef1_pair_of_count_le_two` isolates the pairwise condition under which Round-Robin pure Nash equilibria guarantee EF1. It does not cover envy towards an agent $j$ who appears three or more times in the sequence, which can occur whenever $m > 2n$. Indeed, the counterexample correcting the published claim requires $2n + 2$ goods, where certain agents receive three goods and trigger non-EF1 envy.

The result provides a structural bound: non-EF1 envy in a Round-Robin pure Nash equilibrium can only be directed towards agents who receive at least three goods. When every agent picks at most twice, which occurs when $m \le 2n$, this immediately recovers the global result of `round_robin_pne_ef1_of_card_le_two_mul`.

The result serves as a step towards analyzing picking sequences with $2n + 1$ goods. That question asks whether every Round-Robin pure Nash equilibrium is EF1 when there are $2n + 1$ goods, bridging the gap between the known positive result for $2n$ goods and the $2n + 2$ counterexample.
research: Shows the published claim corrected by arXiv:2610.23686 survives in part: at every Round-Robin pure Nash equilibrium, envy towards any agent with at most two goods is already EF1, for any number of agents (so every equilibrium with at most 2n goods is EF1, while the paper's counterexample has 2n + 2)
